market_context: United States and general English-speaking market
title: Fresh vs. canned tuna: nutrition differences

seo.title: Fresh vs. canned tuna: protein, fat and sodium
seo.meta_description: Fresh yellowfin and canned light tuna are both lean protein foods, but species, packing liquid and salt change calories, fat and sodium. Compare per 100 g.
seo.search_intent: Compare fresh and canned tuna nutrition

excerpt: Raw yellowfin tuna provides about 109 calories, 24.4 g protein, 0.5 g fat and 45 mg sodium per 100 g. A USDA canned-light-in-water reference has 86 calories, 19.4 g protein, 1 g fat and 247 mg sodium. Canned light tuna in oil can approach 198 calories and 8.2 g fat even after draining.
content_html:
Fresh tuna and canned tuna can both be extremely protein-dense, but “tuna” covers multiple species and the can adds another variable: water, oil, broth and salt.

Yellowfin vs. canned light in water

Per 100 gRaw yellowfinCanned light, water, drained
Calories10986
Protein24.4 g19.4 g
Fat0.5 g1.0 g
Sodium45 mg247 mg

The canned reference has about five times as much sodium, while the fresh yellowfin has about 5 g more protein per 100 g.

Oil changes the picture

A USDA canned-light-in-oil reference is around 198 calories and 8.2 g fat per 100 g drained. Draining removes free oil but not every gram retained by the fish.

Species differences matter

Yellowfin, skipjack, albacore and bluefin have different fat and mercury profiles. A comparison between yellowfin steak and skipjack-based canned light tuna is therefore not a pure fresh-versus-canned experiment.

Canning does not eliminate protein

Heat changes texture and can affect some vitamins, but canned tuna remains a concentrated protein food. Water content and species explain part of the per-100-g difference.

How to shop

Look at species, drained weight, packing medium and sodium. Water-packed no-salt-added options minimize added fat and sodium; oil-packed tuna offers a different texture and higher energy density.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: In this comparison, raw yellowfin: 24.4 g/100 g versus 19.4 g for canned light tuna in water.

faq.question: Is canned tuna higher in sodium?
faq.answer: It often is. The reference here has 247 mg/100 g versus 45 mg in raw yellowfin.

faq.question: How much does oil add?
faq.answer: A canned-light-in-oil reference reaches about 198 calories and 8.2 g fat/100 g drained.

faq.question: Are all canned tunas the same species?
faq.answer: No. Canned light, albacore and other products can use different tuna species with different nutrition and mercury levels.
